name: Scott v. Henrich
court: Ninth Circuit (from the District of Montana)
decided: September 9, 1994; opinion withdrawn and revised opinion filed November 2, 1994
topic: Fourth Amendment deadly force, summary judgment where the decedent cannot testify, no least intrusive alternative requirement, relevance of department policy, municipal liability
summary: Two Butte officers responding to reports of a man firing a gun knocked on his apartment door, identified themselves, and shot him when he opened the door holding a long gun pointed at them. The Ninth Circuit affirmed summary judgment for the officers and the municipal defendants. It held that the question is whether the officers acted reasonably, not whether less intrusive alternatives were available, and that department guidelines matter to the Fourth Amendment analysis only when they are meant to protect the person against whom force is used. It also told trial courts how carefully to examine the officer's account when the person shot is dead. It is taught as the deadly force companion to Forrester on the no least intrusive alternative rule.
coverage: The full revised opinion, the order withdrawing the September 9, 1994 opinion, Judge Norris's dissent, and all footnotes were read from the Public.Resource.Org Federal Reporter archive at https://law.resource.org/pub/us/case/reporter/F3/039/39.F3d.912.91-35429.html. The archive file is headed 39 F.3d 912 and carries docket No. 91-35429, which confirms the citation.

The archive text has paragraph numbers but no Federal Reporter page breaks, so no pin cites are given. The dissent's internal references to the majority at pages 914 to 916 are consistent with the citation.
The district court's memorandum and order granting summary judgment (No. CV-87-003-BU, January 3, 1991) was not read. It is described only as the Ninth Circuit and the dissent described it.

Course materials summarize the training point as officers facing a deadly threat not having to try lesser options first. The opinion's least intrusive alternative discussion was directed at the plaintiff's argument about how the officers approached the door, and the dissent notes the widow abandoned her challenge to the shooting itself on appeal. The brief states the holding as the court framed it.
No subsequent history was verified for this brief.
facts:
The facts are as the Ninth Circuit stated them on review of summary judgment, with disputes resolved in the plaintiff's favor. Officers Flamand and Henrich of the Butte-Silver Bow Law Enforcement Agency were called to 701 West Park Street in Butte, Montana, on reports that a man was firing a gun there. A few minutes earlier they had received reports of shots fired at a nearby address. When they arrived, a motel manager pointed to a two-story apartment building across the street that the gunman had entered through a street-level door. A boy told Flamand that he had seen a man fire a shot or a couple of shots, that the man was acting strange or crazy, and that he was staggering. Flamand then saw a man in a second-story window.

The officers quickly approached the street-level door. Henrich banged and kicked the door and yelled words to the effect of "Police, police officers, open up." Flamand stood behind him and covered him. A few minutes later Henrich banged again and identified himself as a police officer. The officers heard fumbling with the lock. The door opened and John Scott stood in the doorway. According to the officers, Scott held a long gun and pointed it at them. Henrich fired a shot that missed. Flamand, apparently believing Scott had fired that shot, fired four shots at Scott, one of which caused the fatal wound. A footnote records that Scott was very intoxicated, with a blood alcohol content of .312.

The dissent adds record facts not disputed by the majority: Scott lived in the building and had called the police twice that day about tenants he was trying to evict, Henrich was among the officers who had spoken with him in person earlier that day, and the gunshots reported were in front of Scott's own building.

Scott's widow sued the officers, the law enforcement agency, the city, and the county under section 1983. On appeal she argued that the officers should have used alternative measures before approaching and knocking on the door, that their conduct violated department guidelines for barricaded suspects, and that the municipal defendants could be liable for inadequate training under City of Canton v. Harris. The district court granted summary judgment to all defendants. The case was submitted without oral argument.
holding:
Affirmed. The court said it was considering "the amount of proof needed to overcome a motion for summary judgment in a deadly force case under section 1983."

The standard. Police may use only force that is objectively reasonable under the circumstances (Graham). Deadly force is reasonable only if the officer has probable cause to believe the suspect poses a significant threat of death or serious physical injury to the officer or others (Garner). Reasonableness must allow for split second judgments in tense, uncertain, and rapidly evolving circumstances.

Summary judgment and qualified immunity. In Fourth Amendment force cases the qualified immunity inquiry is the same as the merits inquiry. Although reasonableness is traditionally a jury question, defendants can still win summary judgment if the court concludes, after resolving all factual disputes in the plaintiff's favor, that the force was objectively reasonable.

The officer as the only surviving witness. The court gave specific direction for deadly force cases: because the officer is often the only surviving eyewitness, "the judge must ensure that the officer is not taking advantage of the fact that the witness most likely to contradict his story" is unable to testify. The judge must carefully examine all the evidence in the record, such as medical reports, the officer's contemporaneous statements, the available physical evidence, and any expert testimony offered by the plaintiff, to determine whether the officer's story is internally consistent and consistent with other known facts. "In other words, the court may not simply accept what may be a self-serving account by the police officer." The court must also look at circumstantial evidence that, if believed, would tend to discredit the officer's story, and consider whether it could convince a rational factfinder that the officer acted unreasonably.

No least intrusive alternative requirement. The plaintiff argued the officers should have used alternative measures before approaching and knocking. The court answered that "the appropriate inquiry is whether the officers acted reasonably, not whether they had less intrusive alternatives available to them." Requiring officers to find and choose the least intrusive alternative "would require them to exercise superhuman judgment," would induce tentativeness, would deter police from protecting the public and themselves, and would entangle courts in endless second guessing of decisions made under stress. "Officers thus need not avail themselves of the least intrusive means of responding to an exigent situation; they need only act within that range of conduct we identify as reasonable." The officers here clearly did: it is hardly unreasonable for officers to take arms, knock on the door, and identify themselves as police when an armed man who recently fired shots and is acting crazy is reported to be inside.

Department policy. Assuming internal guidelines are relevant to reasonableness, they are relevant "only when one of their purposes is to protect the individual against whom force is used." A rule limiting chokeholds or deadly force to protect suspects is germane; a rule banning high speed chases to save gas or protect bystanders is not. The barricaded suspect guidelines here, by their text and context, were meant to safeguard police and other innocent parties, not the suspect. A violation "might be deserving of discipline, but it's irrelevant" to the Fourth Amendment claim.

Municipal liability. Municipal liability does not depend on individual officer liability but does depend on a constitutional violation. Because the officers' decision to enter the building and their use of force fully complied with the Fourth Amendment, there was no violation and no basis for finding the officers inadequately trained (City of Los Angeles v. Heller).

The dissent. Judge Norris would have found triable issues. He read the widow's argument not as a least intrusive alternative claim but as a claim that the decision to rush the door immediately was itself unreasonable because it created an unnecessarily high risk of armed confrontation. He pointed to the plaintiff's expert, who said contemporary practice called for a tactical plan, sealing escape routes, calling for backup, gathering information, and trying to talk the man out, and who said a few questions would have revealed that Scott was the landlord who would have welcomed the police. He also noted the undersheriff's testimony that the barricade guidelines were meant at least in part to protect the suspect, which he said created a triable issue on the relevance of the guidelines.
notDecided:
Whether the shooting itself, once Scott appeared in the doorway with a gun pointed at the officers, was reasonable was not contested on appeal. The dissent states that the widow abandoned her opposition to summary judgment based on what occurred after the officers assaulted the door and relied solely on the approach to the door.

Whether internal police guidelines are relevant to Fourth Amendment reasonableness at all. The court assumed they are and ruled only that these guidelines were not meant to protect the suspect.

Whether the officers' approach violated department policy. The court said a violation would be irrelevant to the claim; it did not decide whether one occurred.

Any theory that officers can be liable for recklessly creating the need to use force. The court addressed the plaintiff's argument as a least intrusive alternative argument and did not analyze provocation or creation of danger as a separate doctrine.
inPractice:
Scott v. Henrich gives officers two rules and one warning.

Rule one: the Fourth Amendment asks whether what you did was within the range of reasonable conduct, not whether something less intrusive was available. The court said requiring officers to find and choose the least intrusive alternative would demand superhuman judgment and would make officers tentative when lives are at stake. That rule covers tactics as well as the trigger pull: here it was applied to the decision to knock on the door with weapons drawn.

Rule two: a policy violation is not automatically a constitutional violation. Department guidelines count in the reasonableness analysis only when they exist to protect the person force is used on. Guidelines written to protect officers and bystanders can get an officer disciplined without making the force unreasonable.

The warning: when the person shot cannot testify, the court will not simply take the officer's word. Judges are told to compare the officer's account against medical reports, contemporaneous statements, physical evidence, and expert testimony, and to look for inconsistencies. An officer's first statement, the scene evidence, and the report must line up.

Dr. Sowards teaches Scott v. Henrich with Forrester as the reasonable, not least intrusive, pair, and adds that California law and policy since 2019 direct officers to consider feasible alternatives and de-escalation. The Ninth Circuit rule and the California expectation coexist: a reasonable option is lawful under the Fourth Amendment even if a gentler one existed, but a California officer should still be able to explain what alternatives were considered and why they were not feasible.
trainIt:
Teach the approach, not just the shot. The contested decision in this case was how to go to the door. Use the scenario as a tactical decision drill: reports of shots fired, a witness who says the man is acting crazy, a figure in an upstairs window, and a street-level door. Have students state what they know, what they do not know, who is at risk if they wait, who is at risk if they go, and what resources are minutes away. Then have them state why the option they chose was reasonable. The court said officers need only act within the range of reasonable conduct; students should be able to show their choice was in that range.

Teach the dissent's list as a planning checklist, not as a legal requirement: gather information, consider containment, call for assistance, and attempt communication when time allows. In Scott the majority held that knocking and announcing was reasonable on those facts; it did not hold that planning is unnecessary.

Teach the evidence lesson for every deadly force encounter. The court told judges to test the surviving officer's story against medical reports, the officer's contemporaneous statements, physical evidence, and expert testimony. Students should understand that what they say at the scene and what the scene shows will be compared against what they write later. Train accurate, timely statements and scene preservation as part of the force response.

Teach policy correctly. Policy violations can end careers. Under Scott they bear on the Fourth Amendment claim only when the policy protects the subject. Students should know both consequences and should not confuse them.
caution: The opinion was read in full from the Public.Resource.Org archive. Pin cites are not given because the archive text has no reporter page breaks. The facts are the summary judgment record as the Ninth Circuit summarized it. The dissent notes that the plaintiff abandoned any challenge to the shooting itself on appeal, so the case should not be taught as a ruling that shooting a man who points a gun at officers is reasonable in every circumstance, even though the majority described the officers' use of force as reasonable and proper.
dissent: Judge Norris dissented. He said the majority mischaracterized the widow's argument. She did not claim that gentler alternatives existed; she claimed that the choice the officers made, storming the door immediately with weapons drawn, was itself unreasonable because it created an unnecessarily high risk of an armed confrontation. He relied on the plaintiff's expert, who said the officers violated the agency's barricaded suspect guidelines and contemporary police practice by failing to make a tactical plan, seal escape routes, call for help, gather information, and try to talk the man out, and who said a few questions would have revealed that Scott was the landlord, had been drinking with the tenants he feared, and would have welcomed police. He also cited the undersheriff's deposition testimony that the guidelines were meant at least in part to protect the suspect, which in his view created a triable issue on the relevance of those guidelines. He would have sent the case to a jury.

applications.title: Reasonable, not least intrusive
applications.body: The court held that officers need not use the least intrusive means of responding to an exigent situation; they need only act within the range of reasonable conduct. This applied to the decision to approach and knock, not only to the decision to shoot.

applications.title: Whose protection is the policy for
applications.body: Department guidelines bear on the Fourth Amendment analysis only when one of their purposes is to protect the person force is used against. Barricade guidelines written to protect officers and the public did not help the plaintiff. A violation may still be a discipline issue.

applications.title: The surviving officer's story gets tested
applications.body: When the person shot is dead, the court said the judge may not simply accept what may be a self-serving account. Medical evidence, physical evidence, contemporaneous statements, and expert testimony are compared against the officer's version. Make sure yours matches the scene.

applications.title: No violation, no municipal liability
applications.body: Because the officers' conduct complied with the Fourth Amendment, the inadequate training claim against the city and county failed. Monell liability requires an underlying constitutional violation.

applications.title: Read the dissent for the tactical lesson
applications.body: The dissent's points about information gathering, containment, backup, and communication did not become law in this case, but they describe the questions an expert and a jury will ask about an approach that ends in a shooting.

quiz.q: According to Scott v. Henrich, what is the appropriate Fourth Amendment inquiry when a plaintiff argues the officers should have done something less intrusive?
options: Whether the least intrusive alternative was used
Whether the officers acted reasonably, not whether less intrusive alternatives were available
Whether the officers followed department policy
Whether the officers waited for a supervisor
quiz.teach: The court said requiring officers to find and choose the least intrusive alternative would demand superhuman judgment and induce tentativeness. Officers need only act within the range of reasonable conduct.

quiz.q: When are internal department guidelines relevant to the reasonableness of force under Scott v. Henrich?
options: Only when one of the guideline's purposes is to protect the individual against whom force is used
Only when the chief testifies about them
quiz.teach: The barricaded suspect guidelines were meant to protect officers and the public, so their violation was irrelevant to the suspect's claim. The court said a violation might deserve discipline but did not bear on the Fourth Amendment question.

quiz.q: What did the court say a judge must do with the officer's account in a deadly force case where the person shot is dead?
options: Accept it, because the officer is the only eyewitness

Carefully examine all the evidence, including medical reports, contemporaneous statements, physical evidence, and expert testimony, to see whether the account is internally consistent and consistent with known facts
Disregard it and deny summary judgment
Send every such case to a jury
quiz.teach: The court said the judge may not simply accept what may be a self-serving account and must look at circumstantial evidence that could discredit it. That is why the officer's first statement and the scene evidence matter so much.
